ogDesc: Bueng Boraphet, Pasan at the source of the Chao Phraya River, Wat Kiriwong, Korea-vibe Ko Yuan, Utthayan Sawan Park and plenty more — 10 Nakhon Sawan attractions with entry fees, parking, and how to plan your trip
eyebrow: Pak Nam Pho locals' picks · Updated 2026
intro: Nakhon Sawan is the gateway to Northern Thailand that most people simply drive through — but if you actually stop, you'll find a city with Thailand's largest freshwater lake, the birthplace of the Chao Phraya River, and the Pak Nam Pho district with its deep Chinese heritage. We've gathered the 10 most talked-about attractions, from riverside landmarks and hilltop temples to city-center parks, a century-old market, and the biggest new mall in the upper central region — all easily covered in a single trip.

🐉 Pak Nam Pho, 12-day Chinese New Year

blocks.html:
When people mention Nakhon Sawan, most think of it as just a stop on the way north — but this city has far more to offer than you'd expect. Its heart is Pak Nam Pho, an old riverside quarter where Chinese settlers put down roots long ago. Wander in any direction and you'll pass shrines, heritage shophouses, and old-school coffee shops mixed in with a brand-new mall. This is where the Ping, Wang, Yom, and Nan rivers merge to form the Chao Phraya, which is why you can clearly see the "two-tone river" at Pasan, the strikingly futuristic curved landmark on the waterfront. Around town there's Bueng Boraphet, the largest freshwater lake in the country; Wat Kiriwong, a hilltop temple with a tower offering 360-degree city views; and leafy public parks like Utthayan Sawan and Ko Yuan, which has been transformed to feel like Korea's Cheonggyecheon canal. Whether you're into nature, temples, photo spots, or malls, there's something here.

What makes Nakhon Sawan special are the stories behind each spot. In winter, Bueng Boraphet fills with thousands of migratory birds, and you can boat through lotus fields or walk the fish tunnel at the aquarium. Pasan is the symbolic monument marking the source of the Chao Phraya River, built thanks to a push from the townspeople themselves. Ko Yuan turned a water-treatment canal into a chill hangout in the middle of the city, complete with over twenty thousand koi you can feed. Central Nakhon Sawan opened with a Chinese Village concept and an LED dragon said to be the longest in Thailand. And during Chinese New Year, Pak Nam Pho hosts its famous 12-day, 12-night deity procession known across the country. If you love a nostalgic wander, there's also the Chum Saeng 100-Year-Old Market on the Nan River, a filming location for the drama Krong Karm. Plan one trip to Nakhon Sawan and you won't be disappointed.

blocks.name: Bueng Boraphet
blocks.signature: Thailand's largest freshwater lake — boat through lotus fields and past waterbirds, visit the waterbird park and fish-tunnel aquarium; gorgeous at dawn and dusk, with flocks of migratory birds in winter
blocks.priceRange: Boat trip ~฿600/boat or ~฿100/person · Aquarium: adults ฿49, children ฿19
blocks.descHtml:
Bueng Boraphet is the largest freshwater lake in Thailand, covering more than 132,000 rai across three districts of Nakhon Sawan — Mueang, Tha Tako, and Chum Saeng. If you love wide-open nature, birdwatching, an easy evening boat ride, or want to bring the family for a stroll and some photos, pin this spot from day one of your trip. It's so vast it feels like visiting a real lake, not just a pond in town.

The highlight everyone talks about is the boat trip through the red lotus fields at Ban Rang Bua on the Tha Tako side. The lotus blooms blanket the water from around 6:00 to 9:30 in the morning before closing up later in the day, and review after review agrees that coming early is the best value — soft light and lotus flowers in full bloom. Birdwatchers should come in the cool season (roughly November–February), when resident waterbirds like Oriental darters and cormorants are joined by migratory flocks that fill the lake. The local boat drivers know all the good spots and will point out birds and nests like true guides. Another must is the 80th Anniversary Aquarium, with its 24-meter fish tunnel, over a hundred species of rare freshwater fish, a touch pool, and a crocodile show arena — great for kids.

Budget-wise it's quite friendly: chartering a boat runs about ฿600 for 10–15 people, or if you're a small group, the Ban Rang Bua community boats cost around ฿100 per person with small children free. The aquarium charges ฿49 for adults and ฿19 for children, open daily around 09:00–16:30. The lake itself and the viewpoints are free to wander, with a large parking lot and several waterfront restaurants and cafes to relax in.

Good to know: check the lotus conditions and water levels with the park's page before setting out, since the red lotus and bird numbers depend on the season and water level. Some periods are quiet and peaceful; winter weekends can get crowded. Bring a hat and sunglasses, and arrive in time for the morning boat rounds to catch both the beautiful light and the cool air before the sun gets strong.
mustOrder: Morning boat trip through the Ban Rang Bua red lotus fields
Winter birdwatching (Oriental darters, cormorants, migratory birds)
The 24-meter fish tunnel at the aquarium
Sunrise and sunset photos over the lake

blocks.name: Pasan (Origin of the Chao Phraya River Monument)
blocks.area: Laem Ko Yom, Pak Nam Pho subdistrict, Mueang Nakhon Sawan district
blocks.signature: A futuristic curved structure at the confluence of the Ping, Wang, Yom, and Nan rivers — the birthplace of the Chao Phraya — and a photo spot for the two-tone river and sunset views
blocks.descHtml:
If you're driving through Nakhon Sawan with a little time to spare, Pasan is the stop to make. It's the symbolic monument marking the source of the Chao Phraya River, set on Laem Ko Yom right at Pak Nam Pho — the exact point where the Ping, Wang, Yom, and Nan rivers converge to become the Chao Phraya. The building is designed as sleek, modern curves sweeping into one another like four streams merging into a single river; the name "Pasan" itself comes from the Thai word "phasan," meaning to merge. It's perfect for architecture photographers, check-in hunters, and anyone looking for a riverside spot to unwind in the evening.

The must-see is the two-tone river view. When the water is high, you can clearly see the Nan (on the right) running reddish-brown while the Ping (on the left) runs green, meeting right at this point. The other tip everyone shares is to come at sunset — the heat eases, the breeze picks up, and the sky changes color behind the curving structure for a gorgeous shot. Stroll around the architecture, watch riverside life on both banks, and find a breezy corner to relax.

Entry is free with no admission fee. There's a wide plaza, convenient parking, and clean restrooms, open daily 06:00–20:00. Many honest reviews agree the building itself is beautiful and modern, but there isn't a lot to keep you occupied for hours — so it suits a photo stop more than a full-day visit. It's popular because it's the city's new landmark: a photo spot, a viewpoint, and the place that tells the origin story of the Chao Phraya River all in one.

Before you go: the midday sun is fairly strong since it's an open riverside plaza, so a hat or umbrella helps. For the clearest two-tone river view, check for high-water periods, and if you're coming for sunset, arrive a bit early to claim a good angle without the crowd.
mustOrder: The curved monument marking the source of the Chao Phraya
The two-tone river view (green Ping, red Nan)
Riverside sunset watching
Photo spots at the four-river confluence
blocks.stayLabel: Well-located places to stay in Nakhon Sawan
blocks.bestFor: Sunset evenings and a quick photo stop while passing through town

blocks.name: Wat Kiriwong and the Nakhon Sawan Observation Tower
blocks.area: Pak Nam Pho subdistrict, Mueang Nakhon Sawan district
blocks.signature: A hilltop temple in the middle of the city with a golden Phra Chulamanee Chedi; climb the 10-story, 32-meter observation tower for 360-degree views over Pak Nam Pho, with stargazing events on some nights
blocks.priceRange: Temple free · small fee for the observation tower
blocks.descHtml:
Wat Kiriwong is the hilltop temple in central Nakhon Sawan that Pak Nam Pho locals regard as the city's guardian temple. It sits atop Khao Daowadueng right in the heart of town, and you can drive all the way up to the parking area — no long stair climbs needed — making it great for merit-makers, view photographers, and families with older relatives in tow. The star here is the Phra Chulamanee Chedi, a gleaming four-story golden chedi on the hilltop visible from far away. Inside, each floor houses Buddha images and replica Buddha footprints for the 12 zodiac years, and the top enshrines relics of the Buddha.

Don't miss climbing to the chedi's top level for a 360-degree view over Pak Nam Pho — you can see the river, the market, and all the way to Bueng Boraphet on a clear day. The other highlight is the Nakhon Sawan Observation Tower, a 10-story structure of about 32 meters in the same compound, with an elevator up to the rooftop deck for full panoramic city views. Many reviews say late afternoon is the prettiest time, when the light softens and the breeze cools, and some nights there are stargazing events on the tower too.

Entry to the temple and chedi is free — donate as you wish — while the observation tower charges a small fee, so the whole visit is very budget-friendly. It's well located opposite Nakhon Sawan Vocational College where Matuli Road meets Daowadueng Road. The temple opens daily around 08:00–17:00, and the observation tower Monday–Friday roughly 10:00–16:30 (check the tower's hours before holiday visits, as it sometimes closes).

It's popular because it packs everything into one spot: paying respects, making merit, and the highest viewpoint in the city, all with an easy climb. Traveler reviews score it consistently well, ranking it among the top attractions in urban Nakhon Sawan. Just two things to know: dress modestly since it's a temple, and if the observation tower is your goal, come on a weekday in the late morning or afternoon to match its opening hours.
mustOrder: Pay respects at the four-story golden Phra Chulamanee Chedi
Climb to the top level for 360-degree city views
Take the elevator up the 10-story (32 m) observation tower
Come in the evening for sunset over Bueng Boraphet

blocks.name: Ko Yuan (Khlong Yuan Chuan Rak)
blocks.signature: A canal-side park transformed from a water-treatment channel into a chill city hangout with Cheonggyecheon vibes — feed over 20,000 koi, see the waterfall weir, street art, and canal-side walkways
blocks.descHtml:
If you thought Nakhon Sawan was just Pak Nam Pho and the Chao Pho Thepharak Shrine, stop by "Ko Yuan" — officially called "Khlong Yuan Chuan Rak" — and you'll be surprised. This is a public space of more than 300 rai in the middle of the city, where the municipality turned a canal fed by the wastewater-treatment system (over 36,000 cubic meters a day) into a long loop of canal-side walkways with a feel reminiscent of Cheonggyecheon in central Seoul. Plenty of people post photos saying it looks like a stroll abroad, even though it's right in the heart of Nakhon Sawan. It's great for families with kids who need to run around, couples on an evening walk, or photographers hunting for fresh angles.

The can't-miss highlight is feeding the fish. The canal water is clean enough to support more than 20,000 koi and native Thai fish (the municipality released them deliberately to prove the treated water really is clean), and when you toss food in, they swarm in dazzling orange-and-white schools — kids love it. Fish food sells for ฿10 a bag right on site. There's also a small waterfall weir with soothing running-water sounds, street-art murals as photo backdrops, canal-side seating, and walkways built with wheelchair-friendly ramps.

It's as budget-friendly as it gets: entry is free with no admission fee, and a bag or two of fish food will keep you entertained for an hour. You can park along the road. It's located in the Nakhon Sawan municipal area on the Ko Yuan side (Pak Nam Pho subdistrict, near where the Ping and Nan rivers meet), easy to reach from downtown. Do double-check the hours, though — on weekdays it usually opens from the afternoon into the evening, while on weekends and holidays it stays open longer, from late morning until late at night.

Tips from people who've been: go in the evening from around 5 pm onward, when the shade and breeze make walking far more pleasant than midday, since the trees aren't yet dense everywhere. Some reviews also warn that the koi are occasionally moved out for care, leaving no fish to see — if feeding the fish is your main goal, check the page or ask locals first. Its Google rating sits at 4.5 from over a thousand reviews, reflecting how much both locals and visitors genuinely enjoy dropping by. All in all, it's a free, worthwhile place to unwind with an overseas feel — no flight required.
mustOrder: Feed the 20,000-plus koi and Thai fish
Photograph the Cheonggyecheon-style canal walkway
See the waterfall weir
Walk the street-art murals
blocks.stayLabel: Well-located places to stay in Nakhon Sawan
blocks.bestFor: Evening strolls, feeding fish with the family, photographers, and budget travelers

blocks.name: Utthayan Sawan Park (Nong Somboon)
blocks.area: Pak Nam Pho subdistrict, Mueang Nakhon Sawan district
blocks.signature: The city's 'green lungs' park with a central lake, a ~3.3 km running loop, and the giant Heavenly Dragon statues at the entrance (fire dragon and water dragon) — a favorite photo spot, best in the early morning and evening
blocks.descHtml:
If you're in downtown Nakhon Sawan looking for somewhere to stretch your legs, Utthayan Sawan — known locally as "Nong Somboon" — is where the townspeople gather almost every evening. It's a large public park of around 314 rai in the heart of the city, with a wide pond in the middle ringed by a shady two-lane loop road lined with big trees — truly the lungs of the city. It suits runners, cyclists, grandparents bringing the kids to feed the fish, and anyone who just wants a breezy spot to sit and relax.

The photo everyone takes is of the giant Heavenly Dragon at the park entrance, flanked by two smaller dragons on each side — a fire dragon and a water dragon — reflecting the Chinese traditions of Pak Nam Pho, a city famous for its deity processions. It's a hugely popular check-in spot that most reviews praise as striking and beautiful, especially in the evening when golden light hits the water. For exercise, the outer loop runs about 3.3 kilometers, with middle and inner loops to match your energy, plus outdoor gym equipment, an aerobics plaza, rest pavilions, and picnic corners dotted around the park.

It's easy on the wallet too — entry and parking are both free. It normally opens around 07:00–18:00, though people keep strolling into the evening and the atmosphere stays lively. At the entrance there's a Punthai coffee shop with both air-conditioned and outdoor seating, and the surrounding area has restaurants, cafes, massage shops, and a mall to continue your day. It's located in Pak Nam Pho subdistrict along the Asian Highway, easy to reach and close to the bus terminal.

One small note: from late morning to noon the sun is fairly strong since the pond area is open, so come at dawn or after 4 pm for the best conditions. Around the end of the year there's sometimes a lantern festival that lights up the whole park — a busier period, but the photos come out especially beautiful.
mustOrder: Photograph the giant Heavenly Dragon at the entrance (fire dragon and water dragon)
Run or cycle the ~3.3 km outer loop around the pond
Relax by Nong Somboon with the breeze at sunset
Grab a coffee at the entrance cafe before or after your walk

blocks.name: Khao No–Khao Kaeo (Wat Khao No)
blocks.area: Ban Daen subdistrict, Banphot Phisai district, Nakhon Sawan
blocks.signature: Twin limestone peaks rising from the rice fields, with macaques waiting for food at the parking lot, hundreds of thousands of bats streaming out of the cave at dusk, and 360-degree views from the summit
blocks.priceRange: Free entry · monkey food and snacks sold for a few dozen baht
blocks.descHtml:
Khao No–Khao Kaeo are two limestone mountains standing alone amid the rice fields along the Nakhon Sawan–Kamphaeng Phet road (Highway 1), visible from far away. What keeps a steady stream of visitors stopping here is how much it packs into one place: troops of macaques, a cave temple with a reclining Buddha, stairways to a summit viewpoint, and the evening highlight — columns of bats streaming out of the cave across the sky. It's a favorite stop for Nakhon Sawan locals and passing travelers alike, since entry is free and no real planning is needed.

At the parking lot you'll be greeted by macaques — a hundred or more waiting for food, with stalls selling monkey feed and snacks for a few dozen baht. Past visitors do warn you to watch whatever's in your hands and bags, as the monkeys are used to people and quick to snatch. If you want to climb to the Buddha's Footprint summit, it's a concrete stairway followed by steel-rung ladders totaling nearly 700 steps, with some stretches almost vertical. Honest reviews say it takes real effort — around 1–2 hours up and down — but the summit rewards you with sweeping 360-degree views over the rice fields. At the base there's also a cave temple with a reclining Buddha to pay respects to.

Entry is free, open daily around 08:00–18:00. If the bats are your goal, come toward dusk: tens of thousands to hundreds of thousands of bats begin streaming out of the Khao Kaeo cave around six in the evening, forming a long dark ribbon across the sky in waves. From downtown Nakhon Sawan, drive toward Banphot Phisai about 45–50 km, roughly 50 minutes; the site sits right on the main road, easy to find, with a parking lot.

Tips from those who've been: if you're climbing, wear grippy shoes and carry water, since the steel-rung sections are steep and hot. Save time in the evening for the bats to make the most of one trip. If you're with small children, stick to the lower sections and the monkeys — the upper stairs aren't suited to little ones — and keep food, plastic bags, and glasses tucked away whenever the monkeys are near.
mustOrder: Feed the macaques at the parking lot (monkey food sold for a few dozen baht)
Wait for the bats streaming out of the cave around six in the evening
Climb the nearly 700 steps to the summit for 360-degree views
Pay respects to the reclining Buddha in the cave temple below
blocks.stayLabel: Well-located places to stay in Nakhon Sawan
blocks.bestFor: Nature and adventure lovers, families who want the kids to see monkeys, and drivers passing through who want a temple, mountain, monkeys, and bats in one stop

blocks.name: Central Nakhon Sawan
blocks.signature: The newest and largest mixed-use mall in the upper central region, built on a Chinese Village concept inspired by the two-tone river, with over 500 brands, an SF cinema, a front park, and a dragon landmark
blocks.priceRange: Free entry · spend as you shop and dine
blocks.descHtml:
If you're in Nakhon Sawan and want somewhere cool to walk, eat well, and take great photos all in one place, Central Nakhon Sawan is the spot practically every Pak Nam Pho household talks about. Opened on 31 January 2024, it's the largest and most complete mixed-use shopping center in the upper central region. The main mall spans 4 floors with hundreds of Thai and international brands, restaurants, cafes, banks, and an IT zone. What sets it apart from other Central branches is its Chinese Village concept, which weaves the story of Pak Nam Pho and the two-tone river (where the Ping and Nan merge into the Chao Phraya) into the design. It works for families with kids and grandparents as well as cafe-hopping, photo-loving teens.

The must-see is the central landmark shaped like a fortune-stick cylinder, surrounded by sculptures and Chinese motifs painted along the walls — grand enough that many reviews call it "beautifully decorated, blending Thai and Chinese styles perfectly." Out front is the Urban Park, over 2 rai with a lantern-lined walkway, a playground, a pet zone, and Longevity Hill, where many come for photos with the dragon. Movie fans can head to the 3rd floor for the SF cinema with its big Zigma Cinestadium screen, 4K laser projection, and Dolby Atmos. For food, the Food Patio gathers Pak Nam Pho favorites alongside big names like Bonchon, BBQ Plaza, MK, and KOI Thé, plus a Tops Market supermarket.

Entry is free — your budget is however much you walk and eat. Parking is plentiful in the front lot and basement (free), open daily 10:00–21:00. It sits in the city center on the Phahonyothin Road side of west Nakhon Sawan, surrounded by government offices, schools, and hospitals, with easy access from several roads. It became a hit fast as the province's first major mall, drawing crowds from opening day, and regularly hosts seasonal events — especially during Chinese New Year, when its dragon parade show is a signature of the dragon city.

Good to know: on long holidays and festival days it gets very crowded and parking fills fast, so come on a weekday afternoon for a relaxed visit. And if you're here for photos of the landmark and the front park, evening — when the lights come on — beats midday.
mustOrder: The central fortune-stick-cylinder landmark with Chinese-Thai motifs
Urban Park out front + the Longevity Hill dragon
The SF cinema on the 3rd floor with the Zigma Cinestadium screen
Food Patio with Pak Nam Pho favorites + Tops Market

blocks.name: Chao Pho Thepharak–Chao Mae Thapthim Shrine and the Pak Nam Pho Chinese New Year Festival
blocks.area: Pak Nam Pho, Mueang Nakhon Sawan district
blocks.signature: A historic shrine at the heart of Pak Nam Pho and the center of the 12-day, 12-night Chao Pho–Chao Mae procession during Chinese New Year, with dragon, lion, and Eng Kor parades and nighttime light spectacles
blocks.priceRange: Free (incense and candles cost a few dozen baht)
blocks.descHtml:
If you want to truly understand the heart of Nakhon Sawan, come to the Chao Pho Thepharak–Chao Mae Thapthim Shrine on the Chao Phraya riverbank opposite Pak Nam Pho market. This red Chinese shrine is over 130 years old (said to have been built around 1870, early in the reign of King Rama V) and enshrines Pun Thao Kong, the deity Guan Yu, and Chao Mae Thapthim, deeply revered by the local Thai-Chinese community. Step inside and you'll find incense smoke, red lanterns, and a steady stream of people praying for fortune and success in business throughout the day. It suits temple-goers, those seeking blessings, and anyone who wants an authentic taste of overseas-Chinese life.

The real highlight comes at Chinese New Year, because this shrine is the center of the "Pak Nam Pho Chao Pho–Chao Mae Procession," the Pak Nam Pho Chinese New Year festival — a tradition passed down for over 100 years (it began around 1917, after the deity was credited with dispelling an epidemic in the city). It runs a full 12 days and 12 nights, with processions carrying the deities around the market accompanied by golden dragon troupes, lion dancers from multiple troupes, the 108 face-painted Eng Kor warriors, Lo Ko drum troupes, martial-arts performers, and a Guan Yin procession. Don't miss the night parade: Eng Kor performers in glowing costumes, fire-wielding lion and dragon dances, capped by spirit mediums walking across fire. The whole city buzzes, with photographers packing the streets.

As for cost, relax — entry and worship are free, and your main spend is a few dozen baht on incense, candles, and offerings. The shrine is open for worship daily during daytime hours (roughly 8 am to evening, sometimes opening very early). The festival falls in late January–February according to the Chinese lunar calendar. It sits in the middle of the old town, easy to reach with parking near the market, and it's close to Pasan, the Chao Phraya-source landmark, so you can combine both in one outing.

It's beloved because it's both a spiritual anchor for locals and a cultural highlight famous nationwide. Most Google reviews score it around 4.6, praising the shrine's sacred beauty, kind staff, and the genuinely grand festival. Just note that during Chinese New Year the crowds are heavy — allow extra time and parking, dress modestly, and mind your belongings in the crush. Outside festival season it's calm and perfect for an unhurried visit.
mustOrder: Pray to Pun Thao Kong and Chao Mae Thapthim
The Chao Pho–Chao Mae procession during Chinese New Year
The nighttime golden dragon, lion, and Eng Kor parades
Photograph the red Chinese shrine on the Chao Phraya riverbank

blocks.bestFor: Worshippers seeking blessings and anyone wanting to see the Pak Nam Pho Chinese New Year festival

blocks.name: Chum Saeng 100-Year-Old Market
blocks.signature: A century-old market on the Nan River with vintage wooden and Sino-colonial buildings next to Chum Saeng railway station, a nostalgic atmosphere, local eats, and filming locations from the drama Krong Karm
blocks.descHtml:
If you're in Nakhon Sawan and want to escape the city for a genuinely old market, the Chum Saeng 100-Year-Old Market is worth setting time aside for. Located in Chum Saeng district about 40 km from downtown, it's a market community on the Nan River that grew up alongside Chum Saeng railway station on the northern line from around 1907. Once a bustling rice-trading hub where Chinese immigrants settled, it left behind a legacy of century-old wooden houses and Sino-colonial shophouses lining the tracks. It's perfect for lovers of nostalgic atmosphere, vintage-photo hunters, and drama fans — it was a filming location for the hit series "Krong Karm," which drew crowds retracing its scenes.

The highlight is slowly soaking in the old buildings and riverside way of life, then digging into affordable local eats. Traveler reviews rave about the market's signature old-style tom yum noodles, the old-Chinese-style rat na with thick glossy gravy at Nai Ko, Je Liang's satay, Je Buay's grilled pork, Je Hung's kuay jab, the pad thai with a queue, Ah Heng's chicken rice, and coconut ice cream to finish. If you fancy walking further, the Hiran Ramit suspension bridge crosses the Nan River for lovely photo views.

It's very easy on the budget: market entry is free and most dishes run about ฿20–60. It sits right by Chum Saeng railway station on the Nan River, and you can park along the roadside. The market opens daily but is liveliest from early morning to late morning — many popular stalls sell out early or close by afternoon, so come early for the fullest selection. On weekends and during the Chum Saeng deity festival (around February and December) it gets especially packed.

Good to know: this is a real living community, not a commercialized theme market. On some weekdays it's quiet, with charm that leans simple rather than flashy. An easy 1–2 hours covers it, and it pairs well with the nearby temples and railway station in one trip. If you love honest old markets with an unpolished atmosphere and cheap, tasty food, this one fits the bill.
mustOrder: Walk the old wooden and Chinese shophouses + Krong Karm filming spots
Old-style tom yum noodles / rat na at Nai Ko
Je Liang's satay + Je Buay's grilled pork
Cross the Hiran Ramit suspension bridge over the Nan River + coconut ice cream
blocks.stayLabel: Well-located places to stay in Nakhon Sawan
blocks.bestFor: Old-market lovers, vintage photo hunters, and Krong Karm fans

blocks.name: Engineer Sheep Farm
blocks.area: Mueang Nakhon Sawan district (suburban zone), Nakhon Sawan
blocks.signature: A sheep farm spanning over 30 rai with animal feeding, farm activities, and meadow-style photo corners — great for kids and photographers
blocks.priceRange: Free entry (feeding grass ฿5 · horse riding/cowboy outfit ฿50)
blocks.descHtml:
Engineer Sheep Farm is Nakhon Sawan's farm-style photo spot, run by the 4th Engineer Battalion at Chiraprawat Military Camp. Its 30-plus rai are laid out as a mixed agro-tourism attraction, ideal for families bringing kids to play with animals and photographers after meadow-and-farm shots without a long drive. The name says sheep farm, but there are actually sheep, goats, horses, wild boars, deer, chickens, ducks, geese, and fish — enough to keep kids entertained all afternoon.

The must-do is feeding the sheep and other animals: buy a bundle of grass for ฿5 and hand it to the sheep right at the fence. For a fun photo, rent a cowboy outfit to pose with the horses, or go for a horse ride for around ฿50. There's also a wooden bridge across the rice paddies, a lotus pond, a vegetable tunnel, flower gardens rotating with the seasons (late year to early year brings especially beautiful blooms), and a vintage-style coffee shop for a cool drink and a rest.

Real reviews consistently mention the fresh air, relaxed atmosphere, plentiful photo corners, and adorable animals kids love — some visitors are regulars because it's close to home and the coffee is good. The best part is free entry: you pay only for feeding grass or optional activities, so the cost per person is very low. An easy 1–2 hours of strolling and photos is well worth it.

It's located inside Chiraprawat Military Camp on the Chiraprawat golf course side, at the boundary of Takhian Luean and Klang Daet subdistricts in Mueang Nakhon Sawan district, open daily 08:00–18:00. Note that the flower fields and greenery change with the seasons, so if you want the blooms at their peak, check the farm's page before going. Late morning or evening, when the sun is gentler, makes for a more comfortable walk and better photo light than midday.

blocks.title: Know before you go in Nakhon Sawan

items.title: Your own car is easiest
items.text: The attractions are spread across town and beyond — Bueng Boraphet and the sheep farm are on the outskirts, so a private or rental car is most convenient. Grab operates in the city but cars are limited; keep the app handy in case rides are hard to find.

items.title: Carry cash
items.text: Chum Saeng 100-Year-Old Market, Pak Nam Pho market, fish food, incense and candles at the shrine, and Bueng Boraphet boat fees are usually cash-only. ATMs are easy to find in town and in the mall.

items.title: Mornings and evenings are best
items.text: Bueng Boraphet, Pasan, and the parks are prettiest in the morning and evening, when the sun is gentle and sunsets are beautiful. Avoid the scorching midday. Note that Ko Yuan opens from the afternoon into the evening on weekdays.

items.title: Chinese New Year is the city's peak
items.text: The Pak Nam Pho Chao Pho–Chao Mae procession during Chinese New Year (January–February) runs 12 days and 12 nights, and the city gets extremely busy with hotels filling fast. If you're coming for the festival, book accommodation several weeks ahead.

items.title: English is limited
items.text: Nakhon Sawan is a mainly Thai city — English menus and signs exist at the mall and major attractions, but most markets and small shops operate in Thai. A translation app or pointing at pictures makes things easier.

items.title: Malls have big free parking
items.text: Central Nakhon Sawan, Pasan, and Utthayan Sawan Park all have free parking lots, while the old market areas have limited spaces. Go early or avoid long holidays for an easier time parking.

blocks.title: How to see Nakhon Sawan in a single day
blocks.html:
Nakhon Sawan's main attractions cluster around the Pak Nam Pho district in town. Start early at Bueng Boraphet before the sun gets strong — take a boat through the lotus fields and past the waterbirds, or walk the fish tunnel at the aquarium. Then head into town to Pasan for the two-tone river, and continue up to Wat Kiriwong to climb the 10-story observation tower for 360-degree views.

Late afternoon into evening is park time: Utthayan Sawan has the giant Heavenly Dragon at its entrance and a running loop around the lake, while Ko Yuan opens in the evening on weekdays — feed the koi with ฿10 bags of fish food and stroll the Cheonggyecheon-style canal. Wrap up with dinner and shopping at Central Nakhon Sawan. And if you're visiting during Chinese New Year, don't miss the Pak Nam Pho Chao Pho–Chao Mae procession — 12 days and 12 nights with the longest dragon and lion parades in Thailand.

With an extra day or a love of nature, drive about 50 km out toward Banphot Phisai to Khao No–Khao Kaeo. Feed the monkeys in the morning, climb the stairs to the summit for 360-degree views over the rice fields, then wait for the hundreds of thousands of bats streaming out of the cave just before six in the evening — a trip-ending sight many never forget.

blocks.text: To enjoy Nakhon Sawan's many spots, base yourself at a well-located hotel in Pak Nam Pho — Bueng Boraphet is a quick morning drive, and the mall and dinner spots are minutes away. We've picked the standout, well-located hotels in Nakhon Sawan for you.

faq.q: Which Nakhon Sawan attractions are unmissable?
faq.a: Three spots define the city: Bueng Boraphet, Thailand's largest freshwater lake with boat trips through lotus fields and past waterbirds; Pasan, the landmark at the birthplace of the Chao Phraya River with two-tone river views and sunsets; and Wat Kiriwong, where the 10-story observation tower gives 360-degree views over Pak Nam Pho. If you visit during Chinese New Year, the Pak Nam Pho Chao Pho–Chao Mae procession is the highlight people travel from across the country to see.

faq.q: What are the highlights of Nakhon Sawan?
faq.a: Nakhon Sawan stands out for its rivers and Chinese heritage. The signature sight is the two-tone river at Pak Nam Pho, where the Ping, Wang, Yom, and Nan rivers meet to form the source of the Chao Phraya. Nature lovers have Bueng Boraphet, which fills with migratory birds in winter; for a relaxed vibe there's Ko Yuan, styled after Korea's Cheonggyecheon canal with over twenty thousand koi to feed; and shoppers get Central Nakhon Sawan, the Chinese Village-concept mall that's the largest in the upper central region.

faq.q: Do Nakhon Sawan attractions charge entry fees?
faq.a: Most are free. Pasan, Utthayan Sawan Park, Engineer Sheep Farm, the Chao Pho Thepharak Shrine, and the malls charge no admission. Ko Yuan is free too — you only pay ฿10 a bag for fish food. The ones with costs are Bueng Boraphet, where boat trips run about ฿600 per boat or around ฿100 per person and the aquarium charges ฿49 for adults and ฿19 for children, and Wat Kiriwong, which is free to enter but charges a small fee for the observation tower.

faq.q: How do you get around Nakhon Sawan, and is parking easy?
faq.a: A private car is the most convenient way to explore Nakhon Sawan, since Bueng Boraphet and the sheep farm are outside town. Grab operates in the city but cars are limited, so keep the app handy. As for parking, spots like Pasan, Utthayan Sawan Park, Wat Kiriwong, and big malls like Central Nakhon Sawan have spacious free lots, while the Pak Nam Pho market area and Chum Saeng 100-Year-Old Market have more limited parking — go early or avoid long holidays.

faq.q: What are the opening hours, and when is the best time to visit?
faq.a: Pasan opens daily around 06:00–20:00 and is best in the evening for the breeze and sunset. Bueng Boraphet is loveliest in the morning or evening when it's cooler, and the cool season (November–February) brings the migratory birds. Ko Yuan opens afternoon-to-evening on weekdays and all day on weekends. The Pak Nam Pho Chinese New Year festival falls during the Chinese New Year period (January–February), the liveliest time of the whole year in the city.
